parts.ask: Bag: counters 5, 10, 20 in ratio 5 : 2 : a; jar: 5 or 10 in ratio 1 : 3. One counter from the bag, two from the jar; R = range of the 3 numbers. Given P(R = 15) = 63/256, form and solve an equation to show a = 9
parts.final_form: a = 9 with at least one further line after the equation
parts.ms: M1 uses a/(a + 7); M1 correct equation, e.g. a/(a + 7) × (1 − (3/4)²) = 63/256; A1* a = 9 with at least one more correct line (MS p.13)
parts.er: Many missed that there are 2 ways of getting 5 and 10 from the jar, or counted 3 ways; once the equation was formed, a further line was needed before the given answer (ER p.5)

parts.ask: Find the sampling distribution of R
parts.ms: B1 ranges 0, 5, 10 (15 given), no extras with non-zero probability; B1 bag probabilities 5/16, 2/16, 9/16; M1 M1 M1 correct method for one, two, three of P(R = 0), P(R = 5), P(R = 10); A1 cao, decimals to 3 d.p. allowed (MS pp.13–14)
parts.er: Many fully correct, often as a table; errors: missing R = 0, or wrong P(R = 5); check that the three probabilities add to 193/256 (ER p.5)

parts.ask: X ~ U[a, b] with P(5 < X < 13) = 1/5 and E(X) = 9: find P(3X > a + b)
parts.ms: M1 (a + b)/2 = 9 and 8/(b − a) = 1/5 (a = −11, b = 29); M1 realise P(X > 6) is needed; A1 23/40 (MS pp.15–16)
parts.er: Many found a = −11, b = 29 then stopped, not seeing that P(X > 6) was needed; a sketch of the uniform distribution would have helped (ER p.5, reported as (a))

parts.ask: Y ~ U[1, c] with Var(Y) = 0.48: find the exact value of E(Y²)
parts.er: Many found c = 3.4, but often by expanding (c − 1)²/12 and solving a quadratic; errors: 0.48 − E(Y²), or not squaring E(Y) (ER p.5, reported as (b))

parts.ask: A 20 cm wire is cut at a random point; the longer piece is cut in half: find P(the shortest of the 3 pieces is under 6 cm)
parts.final_form: 4/5 (any answer of 4/5 from correct working scores 5/5)
parts.ms: M1 identify a correct region, e.g. W < 6 or W > 14 or 8 < W < 12 (W ~ U[0, 20]); M1 one correct probability; M1 a second; dM1 combine, e.g. 3/10 + 3/10 + 1/5; A1 cao 4/5. Alternatives: 1 − P(6 < W < 8) − P(12 < W < 14), or conditional on W < 10 (MS pp.15–16)
parts.er: By far the hardest question; many showed little grasp of the context; not defining the distribution used hindered attempts; best routes used X ~ U[10, 20] or Y ~ U[0, 10] (ER p.5, reported as (c))

parts.ask: Shoes are sold at a mean rate of 4 pairs per hour on a weekday: suggest a suitable distribution for sales per hour
parts.ms: B1 Poisson and 4, seen in (a); "P(4)" not allowed (MS p.7)
parts.er: Strong start; the most common problem was omitting the parameter 4 (ER p.3)

parts.ask: State one assumption needed for this model
parts.final_form: pairs of shoes sold singly / randomly / independently / at a constant rate
parts.ms: B1 assumption in context of shoes or sales (MS p.7)
parts.er: Mostly right idea; some gave no context (ER p.3)

parts.ask: Find P(more than 4 pairs sold in an hour) and P(more than 4 sold in each of 3 consecutive hours)
parts.er: (i) common error 1 − P(X ≤ 3); (ii) most cubed (i); rare errors were ×3, and N(12, 12) with P(X > 4) (ER p.3)

parts.ask: After an advert, 7 pairs are sold in one hour: test at 5% for an increase in sales, stating hypotheses
parts.final_form: H0: λ = 4, H1: λ > 4; P(X ≥ 7) = 0.1107 > 0.05 (or CR X ≥ 9); not significant; no evidence of an increase
parts.ms: B1ft hypotheses in λ or µ; M1 1 − P(X ≤ 6) (CR: 1 − P(X ≤ 8) = 0.0214); A1 awrt 0.111 or CR X ≥ 9; M1 consistent statement; dA1 contextual conclusion not rejecting H0, with the key words (MS p.7)
parts.er: Well done; rare hypothesis errors (in words, or using 7); most found 0.1107; errors 1 − P(X ≤ 7) and P(X = 7) (ER p.3)

parts.ask: A bag of many 20p and 50p coins; sample of 3: list all possible combinations
parts.ms: B2 all four (B1 for three); repetitions ignored (MS p.8)
parts.er: Generally correct (most gave all 8 permutations); a few ignored "list" and drew a tree (ER p.3)

parts.ask: The mean X̄ takes values 20, a, b, 50 with P(20) = 4913/8000 and P(50) = 27/8000: write down a and b
parts.ms: B1 both (MS p.8)
parts.er: Generally correct (ER p.3)

parts.ask: P(20p) = p, P(50p) = q: find p and q
parts.er: Generally correct (ER p.3)

parts.ask: Hence find c = P(X̄ = 30) and d = P(X̄ = 40)
parts.ms: M1 3p²q or 3pq² with their values; M1 both (or c + d = 1 − others); A1 both (MS p.8)
parts.er: The one (rare) major problem was omitting the binomial coefficient 3 (ER p.3)

parts.ask: M = mode of the 3 coins: find the sampling distribution of M
parts.ms: B1 values 20 and 50 only; M1 4913/8000 + c or 27/8000 + d; A1ft both, summing to 1 (MS p.8)
parts.er: Hardest part: some found the median instead; some gave 1/2 each or did not add c and d; usual loss was wrong c, d without noticing the sum ≠ 1 (ER p.3)

parts.ask: 10% of tennis balls fail a bounce test; sample of 10: find P(at least 4 fail) and P(more than 1 but fewer than 5 fail)
parts.er: Inequalities badly handled by some: (i) 1 − P(X ≤ 4); (ii) many off-by-one versions and mixed forms such as P(X ≤ 4) − (1 − P(X ≤ 1)) (ER pp.3–4)

parts.ask: After process changes, 2 of 50 balls fail: test at 5% whether this supports the claim of a reduced failure probability
parts.final_form: H0: p = 0.1, H1: p < 0.1; P(X ≤ 2) = 0.1117 > 0.05 (or CR X ≤ 1); not significant; claim not supported
parts.ms: B1 hypotheses in p or π; B1 awrt 0.112 or CR X ≤ 1; M1 consistent statement (needs a p-value or CR); A1 contextual conclusion not rejecting H0; no hypotheses → A0 (MS p.9)
parts.er: Errors as in Q1(d): P(X < 2) or P(X = 2) used; many clear contextual conclusions (ER p.4)

parts.ask: In a second sample of n balls none fail, and the claim is supported at 1%: find the smallest n
parts.er: Not all found 0.9ⁿ < 0.01; a few did not reverse the inequality when dividing by ln0.9 and got 43; trial and improvement worked; tables users compared only 40 and 50 (ER p.4)

parts.ask: X has a rectangular pdf of height π/20 from k to 21k (diagram): find P(X < 10k)
parts.er: Often correct, but many left 9πk/20, which must be simplified to a number (ER p.4)

parts.ask: Show that k = 1/π
parts.ms: M1 (21k − k)(π/20) = 1 (20k allowed); A1* fully correct (MS p.10)
parts.er: Well answered using total area 1; a few integrated (ER p.4)

parts.ask: Find E(X) and Var(X) in terms of π
parts.ms: B1 11/π; M1 (21k − k)²/12 or integration; A1 100/(3π²). SC answers left in k: B1M1A0 (MS p.10)
parts.er: A significant minority did not simplify the variance, often forgetting to square k or 20 (ER p.4)

parts.ask: Circles have area A = π(X + 2/π)²: find E(A)
parts.ms: M1 expand to π[E(X²) + 4E(X)/π + 4/π²] or set up ∫A f(x)dx; M1 E(X²) = Var + E(X)² = 463/(3π²) (or integration); M1 substitute (or limits); A1 607/(3π) (MS p.10)

parts.er: Often fully correct; errors were arithmetic slips in c, F(3) = 1, and setting integrals of each cdf piece equal to 1 (ER p.5)

parts.ask: Find the value of b
parts.ms: M1 continuity at 5 (F(5) = 1/4) or at 9 (F(9) = 7/12), ft (a); A1 cao (MS p.10)
parts.er: Usually more successful, by either method (ER p.5)

parts.ask: Find P(6 < Y ≤ 9), showing working
parts.ms: M1 F(9) − F(6); M1 substitute into F with their b; A1 1/4 (MS p.10)
parts.er: Mostly straightforward; inequality errors such as F(9) − F(7) (ER p.5)

parts.ask: Specify the pdf f(y) for 5 < y ≤ 9
parts.er: Almost all scored this (ER p.6)

parts.ask: Given ∫₃⁵(6y − 5)f(y)dy + ∫₉¹⁰(6y − 5)f(y)dy = 26.5, find E(6Y − 5), making the method clear
parts.ms: M1 ∫(6y − 5)(1/12)dy; dM1 integrate; dM1 26.5 + ∫ from 5 to 9; A1 awrt 38.8. SC answer only, or not using the given information, M0M1M1A1 (MS p.10)
parts.er: Main problem was ignoring "Using the information" (some verified it instead); many used (6y − 5)(y − 2)/12, i.e. F instead of f (ER p.6)

parts.ask: W ~ U[a, b] with P(W > 17) = 1/5 and P(W < k) = 53/60: find P(17 < W < k)
parts.er: Caused the most difficulty: success came from P(W < k) − P(W < 17) or a diagram; some used P(W > 17) in place of P(W < 17) (ER p.6)

parts.ask: Var(W) = 75: find a and b
parts.ms: B1 (b − a)²/12 = 75; B1 a probability equation, e.g. (b − 17)/(b − a) = 1/5; M1 eliminate b − a (= 30); A1 both (MS p.11)
parts.er: Most got the variance equation; good solutions saw b − a = 30 at once, others solved quadratics and had to reject a root (ER p.6)

parts.ask: Find the value of k
parts.ms: M1 (k + 7)/30 = 53/60 or equivalent, ft; A1 19.5 (MS p.11)
parts.er: Generally found by those correct in (b)(i); ft credit needs method shown (ER p.6)

parts.ask: Find P(−5 < W < 5)
parts.er: Partial credit from wrong a, b only when working was shown (ER p.6)

parts.ask: Find E(W²)
parts.ms: M1 Var(W) + E(W)² = 75 + 8² (or ∫w²/(b − a)); A1 139 (MS p.11)
parts.er: Routine for most; some forgot to square the mean or made sign slips (ER p.6)

parts.ask: Muffins sold singly at a mean of 8 per hour: find P(at least 4 but not more than 8 in a random hour)
parts.er: Good source of marks; inequality errors P(X ≤ 7) − P(X ≤ 3) or P(X ≤ 8) − P(X ≤ 4) (ER p.7)

parts.ask: 5 random non-overlapping half-hours: find P(fewer than 3 muffins sold in exactly 2 of them)
parts.er: Most found 0.2381 but many did not know what to do next (some squared it); many fully correct (ER p.7)

parts.ask: Given 4 muffins sold in an hour, find P(more sold in the first 15 minutes than in the last 45 minutes)
parts.ms: M1 a correct product, e.g. P(W = 4)P(X = 0) with W ~ Po(2), X ~ Po(6); M1 divide by P(R = 4) from Po(8); M1 complete expression; A1 13/256. Alternative: number in first 15 min ~ B(4, 0.25), P(F = 3) + P(F = 4) (MS p.12)
parts.er: Most discriminating part; many only tried "3 then 1"; some used P(R = 4) as the denominator with a wrong numerator, e.g. P(X ≥ 3) × P(X ≤ 1); the binomial route was efficient for the few who used it (ER p.7)

parts.er: Mostly correct; a few gave 64a (the height) as the mode (ER p.3)

parts.command: Use algebraic integration to show that

parts.ask: T-shirts: 20% small at £10, 30% medium at £12, 50% large at £15: find the mean value
parts.er: Answered well by virtually all (ER p.4)

parts.ask: A random sample of 3 T-shirts: list all possible combinations of the individual selling prices
parts.ms: B1 at least 5 combinations; B1 all 10 (repeats ignored) (MS p.9)
parts.er: Usually fine when "individual selling prices" was read correctly; the usual omission was 10 12 15; listing sizes (S M L) instead gained no credit (ER p.4)

parts.ask: Find the sampling distribution of the median selling price of the 3 T-shirts

parts.er: Conditions known but often given without the context of complaints, losing the mark (ER p.5)

parts.ask: Find P(fewer than 3 complaints) and P(at least 6 complaints) in a given week
parts.er: (i) mostly correct; (ii) a few used 1 − P(X ≤ 6) and lost both marks (ER p.5)

parts.ask: 12 complaints in a random week: test at 5% whether the mean exceeds 6 per week, stating hypotheses
parts.final_form: H0: λ = 6, H1: λ > 6; P(X ≥ 12) = 0.0201 < 0.05 (or CR X ≥ 11); significant; mean number of complaints greater than 6 per week
parts.ms: B1 hypotheses in λ or µ; M1 1 − P(X ≤ 11) (or CR via 1 − P(X ≤ 10)); A1 0.0201 or CR ≥ 11; M1 correct non-contradicting statement; A1ft contextual conclusion with key words (MS p.10)

parts.command: Use a suitable approximation to test
parts.ask: 26 complaints in 6 weeks after changes: using a suitable approximation, test at 5% whether the mean is now less than 6 per week
parts.final_form: H0: λ = 6 (36), H1: λ < 6; N(36, 36); P(Y ≤ 26) ≈ P(Z < −1.583) = 0.0571 > 0.05 (or CR < 25.6); not significant; no evidence mean fell below 6 per week
parts.ms: B1 hypotheses (36 allowed); B1 N(36, 36); M1 standardise with 25.5/26/26.5 (or CR with −1.6449); M1 continuity correction 26.5; A1 awrt 0.057 or CR < 25.6; M1 correct statement; A1ft contextual conclusion. Exact Poisson (0.0513) scores M0M0A0 (MS p.10)
parts.er: N(36, 36) often used, but N(6, 6) lost the next 3 marks; many standardised correctly, but too many used no continuity correction (ER p.5)
